title: A named compliance obligation
text: Is the company subject to a named regulatory obligation or deadline it must meet — NIS2, DORA, ISO 27001, PCI DSS?
instructions:
Counts: a named regulation or framework with a deadline, an audit requirement, or a certification programme the company says it is working towards.

Does not count: a vendor explaining what the regulation means in general, or an article about the regulation with no connection to this company's own obligations.

title: A reported security incident
text: Has the company suffered a breach, attack or security enforcement action?
instructions:
Counts: a reported breach, ransomware incident, data leak, regulatory fine or enforcement action that names this company.

Does not count: industry-wide statistics, a same-named company, or a breach at a supplier reported as a general news item.

title: Building security operations in-house
text: Does the company sell security operations as a service, or run its own as a product of its own?
instructions:
Counts: the company sells security operations, managed detection or a security product of its own. That is a provider of the capability rather than a buyer of it, so it counts against calling them.

Does not count: a company running an internal security team, or a security operations centre of its own. Most large enterprises have one; it does not stop them buying incident response, compliance work or specialist engineering.

title: A new security leader
text: Has the company appointed a new CISO, head of security or equivalent security leader?
instructions:
Counts: a named appointment or promotion into a role that owns security for the whole organisation, announced publicly.

Does not count: a security engineer hire, a vendor's own staff, or a role below director level. A new security leader reviews the inherited stack, which is a buying moment.

title: A data or AI initiative
text: Has the company started a data, analytics or AI initiative with a named use case?
instructions:
Counts: a named AI or data programme, a named use case in production or pilot, or a stated ambition with a business owner attached.

Does not count: a vendor case study about someone else, a generic "we are exploring AI" statement with no use case, or a prediction about the industry.

title: Selling a data or AI platform of its own
text: Is the company a vendor of data, analytics or AI platforms rather than a buyer of them?
instructions:
Counts: the company describes a data, analytics or AI product of its own that customers buy, or positions itself as a provider of the capability this question looks for in a buyer. A vendor writes about its own category constantly, so its pages outrank a real buyer's and it lands in the queue on its own marketing.

Does not count: a company that has built an internal data team to run platforms it bought.

title: A platform migration under way
text: Is the company migrating a core platform — ERP, core banking or a data platform?
instructions:
Counts: a named migration with a destination or a deadline. A migration is the moment a buyer is forced to re-examine the processes around the system, which is when services get bought.

Does not count: a vendor announcing a product.

title: An AI governance mandate
text: Has the company stood up AI governance, a responsible-AI policy or an AI risk function?
instructions:
Counts: a named AI governance body, a responsible-AI policy, or work to meet the EU AI Act. It precedes the spend: a company that has to govern models has to know what models it runs.

Does not count: a think-piece about AI risk.

title: A data governance programme
text: Is the company running a data governance, quality or master-data programme?
instructions:
Counts: a named governance or data-quality programme, a master data management initiative, or a stated single-source-of-truth programme.

Does not count: a general statement that data is important.

title: Hiring data or ML staff
text: Is the company hiring data, analytics or machine-learning staff?
instructions:
Counts: open roles for data engineering, analytics engineering, data science or machine learning inside this company.

Does not count: a consultancy advertising data roles for client projects, or a role that is not part of this company's own function.

title: A cost-reduction programme with a target
text: Has the company announced a cost-reduction or efficiency programme with a quantified target?
instructions:
Counts: a stated programme to cut cost, headcount or the cost base, with a number attached — a percentage, an amount, or a number of roles. The brief names this signal directly: a quantified target is what turns a vague efficiency ambition into a budget.

Does not count: generic cost pressure in a results story, or a bank analyst's estimate.

title: Hiring for process excellence
text: Is the company hiring for automation, RPA, process-mining or process-excellence roles that select, govern or manage automation rather than build it?
instructions:
Counts: roles whose job is to choose, govern, roll out or manage automation across the business — process excellence, process mining, automation programme lead, RPA business analyst, centre of excellence roles. Hiring for high-volume manual processing work also counts, because that is the work automation replaces.

Does not count: a role that writes automation code as a product for external customers, or an internship. A vendor hiring RPA engineers is building, not buying.

title: Building automation in-house
text: Does the company sell automation, or build it as a product of its own rather than buying the capability?
instructions:
Counts: the company states it sells or provides automation to others, runs an internal automation factory as a business, or has an automation product of its own. This is a company that will build rather than buy, so it counts against calling them.

Does not count: a company that has an internal team overseeing external delivery partners, or that hires, uses or runs automation inside its own business. Internal capability is the normal state of a large company and is often exactly the buying signal we are looking for.
counterCues: what is a centre of excellence

title: An announced efficiency programme
text: Has the company announced an efficiency, cost-reduction or process-optimisation programme with a quantified target?
instructions:
Counts: a named programme, a stated financial or headcount target, or a public commitment to reduce cost per transaction, consolidate shared services, or remove manual processing.

Does not count: a generic statement that the company "invests in digital", a product page, or a supplier's description of work it did for someone else. The programme must belong to this company and must be current.

title: Consolidating shared service centres
text: Is the company consolidating shared service centres or business services into a captive operation?
instructions:
Counts: moving scattered finance, HR or IT operations into one shared service centre, a global business services organisation, or a captive centre — the classic precursor to an automation programme, because consolidation is what makes volume worth automating.

Does not count: a company selling shared-service outsourcing to others.

title: Adopting process mining
text: Is the company adopting process mining, task mining or process intelligence?
instructions:
Counts: a named process-mining platform or a stated process-discovery programme. Naming the tooling is the strongest form of this signal, because it means the budget is already approved.

Does not count: a vendor describing its own product to the market.

title: Already committed to an automation vendor
text: Does the company already run a multi-year automation programme with a named vendor, which would make switching unlikely?
instructions:
Counts: a signed multi-year agreement, a named strategic partner for automation, or a contract renewal or extension with a specific supplier.

This is counter-evidence, not a disqualifier: a company with an incumbent partner is harder to sell to, but the research says prior vendor experience is also the strongest predictor of buying again, so it reduces the score rather than removing the company.
